implementation_notes: The Rails-era realization is a plain old Ruby object whose collaborators arrive through the constructor and whose single public call/execute method runs one use case; the transaction boundary is the ActiveRecord class-method block - ActiveRecord::Base.transaction do ... end - which commits on normal exit and rolls back when an exception is raised. Record integration events in an outbox inside the block and let an after_commit relay publish them; ActiveRecord::Rollback is swallowed, while any other exception is re-raised. Step-pipeline gems (dry-transaction) are an alternative packaging when a use case is best expressed as a sequence of steps returning success/failure.
pitfalls: Wrong move: raise ActiveRecord::Rollback for a caller-visible business failure; failure: the block rolls back but swallows that exception and looks successful; instead: raise a domain/application error and translate it at the boundary.
Wrong move: publish to a broker inside the transaction; failure: the broker side effect cannot roll back with the database; instead: record an outbox row and publish from an after_commit relay.
Wrong move: assume rollback restores saved Ruby objects; failure: in-memory instances still contain post-write state even though the database reverted; instead: discard or reload them after rollback.
